back: False. When using floating point literals, always include at least one decimal place (even if the decimal is 0). This helps the compiler understand that the number is a floating point number and not an integer.
front: True or False: when using a float data type, you don't need to include one decimal place if the value is a whole number.
source_suffix:
int a { 5 }; // 5 means integer
double b { 5.0 }; // 5.0 is a floating point literal (no suffix means double type by default)
float c { 5.0f }; // 5.0 is a floating point literal, f suffix means float type
int d { 0 }; // 0 is an integer
double e { 0.0 }; // 0.0 is a double
Note that by default, floating point literals default to type double. An f suffix is used to denote a literal of type float.Best practiceAlways make sure the type of your literals match the type of the variables they’re being
source_text: When using floating point literals, always include at least one decimal place (even if the decimal is 0). This helps the compiler understand that the number is a floating point number and not an integer.
